Check one two — "space cadet to mothership, coming over." Hey what's up good people of the internet, it's your old buddy KK. Thanks for following along on all these video blogs and podcasts I've been putting out lately. I've been trying to put all the infrastructure in place to layer a bunch of interesting stuff that's coming next on top of it, so I appreciate it. If you're a friend or a colleague, help me out — send this podcast to other people, get them to subscribe to my YouTube, help me build this audience and grow from there.

So anyway, I am headed from my cabin on Hornby Island this morning off to my studio at the Hornby Spar Makerspace, and I've really come to enjoy these little talks and drives to do story time. Today's story time is going to be about Burning Man. It's that time of year again and all the peeps are packing on up and washing the dust off last year's gear and heading down to Black Rock City, Nevada for the world's biggest do-it-yourself art experience. I'm not going this year — always a bit of a bummer, but it's a big effort with me trying to move to Vancouver and get some of these companies off the ground, so it's just not the right time. But I'm sending my love and support to all the crews heading down there, and I can't wait to see what you get up to.

I've been publishing a bunch of photo essays from previous years, and that's the kind of stuff I want to talk about today. I've been really lucky with my Burning Man experience. I heard about it first in 1998 when I was running Spark Online magazine back in the day, and it intrigued me — we were able to cover the event for the magazine, but I was not able to go. Flash forward to 2005: me and Kim Cathers decided Burning Man was in our future and we bought tickets and planned to go, but one thing led to another, we weren't on the same page, and when Burning Man rolled around that didn't happen.

A few years later — maybe like 10, to be exact — I was down at the Okeechobee Music Festival with Tyler Hanson and his whole crew, the Kulture House crew, and we were building all the tea lounge and freaky art experiential stuff for what is otherwise a bigger music festival. And I met this strange cat, Uncle Charlie, a Burning Man OG. He's been building large steel monuments and sculptures out there at Burning Man since the beginning of time, I think — like 20 years or more — and he's well known in the art world and in the Burning Man world. He and I connected really hard at Okeechobee. He had brought out this exhibit called the Fleeble [Flobbler] — a huge eight-seated steel flaming teeter-totter that eight people could ride at a time and get it all rocking and rolling, and I got to control the flame effects and just hang with this crew. It was really awesome.

It was so awesome that the next year at Okeechobee I decided to switch camps and move from the VIP Kulture House art support camp into camp with Uncle Charlie and his ragtag band of merry scallywags. That formed a friendship, and Charlie invited me to join his Burning Man crew. He runs a camp called ASS Camp — which is perfect for me — Art Support Services. And he asked me to be the documentarian of their build.

They were building a huge 50-foot-tall metal sculpture. It was also a teeter-totter, but instead of eight seats on it there were two platforms on each side — you get like 30 of your friends to stand on one of the two sides of the platform and get the thing a-rocking. It took a lot of work and it was pretty dangerous, but a good time was had by all. You could fill it full of two cords of firewood and we burned it three or four times during the Burning Man week. So the whole team of us — like 40 — after this thing was constructed would load up the truck with wood and drive the wood out to the sculpture, crawl inside the sculpture and load it all up with wood, and start fire at the beginning of the night.

Also we would accept donations of meats and sausages, which we would put in the cock's ass, and after a night of shenanigans and riding the red hot ride, we'd flip the old poop chute open and I would fall out hundreds of freshly-done meat sticks ready to feed the people as the sun rose. Totally incredible experience. I got to go three weeks early with Charlie, when Black Rock City hadn't even been built yet — none of the streets are up, and then the street signs go up, and you get to build and watch the city being built and all the art projects around you. By the time Burning Man rolls around it feels like you've done and seen it all, and I shifted into a down gear once Burning Man rolled around and pretty much just hung out at camp and held court, let people wander on through, took them out to the sculpture. They had a really unique and awesome Burning Man experience.

Uncle Charlie and I have stayed connected over the years. We've been some support to each other on a sobriety journey that we're on, and he's a good man who I love a lot, who has the most awesome community of collaborators and other artists that would just bend over backwards to help him achieve any creative dreams. So Charlie, I love you man, and I can't wait till we can work together on something big and awesome.

Oh, another thing — it's always nice to have a role, and being the photographer was awesome but it wasn't quite enough to make me feel like I was contributing. So Charlie saw that I was responsible, organized and a leader, and he asked me to be quartermaster of the whole project. What the quartermaster does in the military — they're the guys that make sure all the supplies and tools are on hand and safe and sharp and gassed up and ready to go. Charlie flipped me the keys to two semi trucks and I became the guy in charge of making sure everything was where it was supposed to be when it was supposed to be there. If someone couldn't find something, I would probably know where it was. It was an awesome role for a guy who's great at observation and likes to know everything that's going on out there, and I was super grateful to flex my muscles in that way.

I also, at Okeechobee, met another guy called Tyson Ayers and his partner — let's call her Leah Desjardins, even though I'm not sure that's how you say her last name. This is the sweetest couple. They're musicians and educators, and Tyson's got a really cool concept for building sound caves — immersive rooms made out of the harps extracted from grand pianos, where you can perform or listen to music. Leah does tea ceremonies and they're really quite incredible. The five walls of the pentagram sound cave are built with these piano harps, and then the roof is built of piano harps, and the resonance in there is incredible.

Experimenting with those sound caves led Tyson to dream big, and so he conceived of a large-scale project that combined five sound caves together with a huge pagoda into a sculpture called The Shrine of Sympathetic Resonance. Sympathetic resonance is a really cool musical concept where the sound vibrations from one thing resonate or make vibrations in another thing. One thing I think of is when I'm driving down the road in my truck and there's a load tied down and the strings/ropes are tight — as you drive, those strings start to vibrate like a low-frequency guitar string. In fact, if you put one twist in that rope, the sound that string makes goes up an octave; two twists, up two octaves; three twists, up three octaves — as you shorten the wavelength the sound changes. Anyway, the sound cave was tuned to the resonant frequency of the earth.

Over the course of a year we collected 55 grand pianos from around Oakland and San Francisco. We essentially turned half of our crew into movers, driving through, picking up people's busted instruments and bringing them back to our warehouse and taking them apart. With a team of 50 or 60 collaborators we were able to construct a 50-foot-tall sympathetic-sound-resonant pagoda and then transport that to Burning Man and build it again. We got to show up super early, be with a crew of exceptional do-it-yourself badasses and makers, and a real community was formed around the building of that project. The sculpture in the end was incredible — so many different things happened there: concerts happened there, weddings happened there, people making love, sleeping out, photo shoots. It was just a beautiful space.

And unlike Uncle Charlie's Red Hot Cock — because the Shrine of Sympathetic Resonance was made of wood — in Burning Man tradition we got to burn it to the ground. Our buddy Ian Tuma led a big burn crew; we disassembled all the paints and electronics and toxic things from it, and the night before the Man burned, we had thousands of people assembled in a perimeter around the shrine to watch it burn.

I'll try to drop some photos of these projects into the video. Those of you who know me know I'm not that good at editing stuff — I like to do one-take wonders. There are lots of other Burning Man stories trapped inside those two things, but that's the stuff I wanted to share with you for now and put down on the permanent record. I'd love to hear what you guys want me to talk about — I've got all sorts of things on my brain, a mix of future stuff I'm working on and past stories of projects and companies that have never seen the light of day. Thanks for following along and tuning in and supporting me. If you've got cool stuff you're up to, get in touch — I love doing my weekly community shout-outs. Kris Krüg from Hornby Island, over and out for now, internet.
